extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of art history, practicing painters/sculptors/architects, and patrons interested in Renaissance standards of artistic quality
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and aesthetic standards (rule, order, proportion, draughtsmanship, manner, finish, colouring, invention, etc.) used in Vasari's Lives to judge and describe the quality of architecture, painting, and sculpture in the Renaissance. The page provides descriptive definitions and exemplars (Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, Correggio, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule (architecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule, then, in architecture, was the process of taking measurements from antiquities and studying the ground-plans of ancient edifices for the construction of modern buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured study of ancient examples (antiquities, ground-plans) as the basis for designing modern buildings; borrow proportions and formal solutions from the classical past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order (architectural orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order was the separating of one style from another, so that each body should receive its proper members, with no more interchanging between Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Tuscan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinctness of classical orders; avoid mixing elements across Doric/Ionic/Corinthian/Tuscan inappropriately—each should retain its proper members and relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion was the universal law applying both to architecture and to sculpture, that all bodies should be made correct and true, with the members in proper harmony; and so, also, in painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure harmonious relations among parts of a figure or building; proportion is a universal organizing law across media. A later passage notes the need for a 'certain correctness of judgment' to achieve grace without mechanical measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draughtsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Draughtsmanship was the imitation of the most beautiful parts of nature in all figures, whether in sculpture or in painting; and for this it is necessary to have a hand and a brain able to reproduce with absolute accuracy and precision, on a level surface--whether by drawing on paper, or on panel, or on some other level surface--everything that the eye sees; and the same is true of relief in sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate observational drawing is essential—precise reproduction of nature's forms, muscles, and details on a flat surface or in relief. Examples: improved drawing in Verrocchio, Mantegna, Signorelli, Leonardo.

rubrics_metrics.name: The beautiful manner (manner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manner then attained to the greatest beauty from the practice which arose of constantly copying the most beautiful objects, and joining together these most beautiful things, hands, heads, bodies, and legs, so as to make a figure of the greatest possible beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create an idealized 'beautiful manner' by selectively combining and copying the best parts observed in nature and earlier works to compose figures of maximum beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom within rule and invention
rubrics_metrics.description: There was wanting in their rule a certain freedom which, without being of the rule, might be directed by the rule and might be able to exist without causing confusion or spoiling the order; which order had need of an invention abundant in every respect...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance adherence to classical rules with inventive freedom—rule provides structure, but invention and creative liberty are required to enrich and enliven work without breaking order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of judgment in proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: There was wanting in their proportion a certain correctness of judgment, by means of which their figures, without having been measured, might have, in due relation to their dimensions, a grace exceeding measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop an aesthetic judgment to achieve graceful proportions without relying solely on mechanical measurement; the eye and judgement refine proportion into grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish / minuteness of finish
rubrics_metrics.description: They also lacked that minuteness of finish which is the perfection and bloom of art... That finish, and that certain something that they lacked, they could not achieve so readily, seeing that study, when it is used in that way to obtain finish, gives dryness to the manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek delicate, finalizing detail in hands, feet, hair, beards, and surfaces to achieve the 'bloom' of art—but beware that overworked study can make a manner dry; finish should bring delicacy and vivacity rather than stiffness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy, plumpness, and grace of flesh
rubrics_metrics.description: They also lacked... the delicacy that comes from making all figures light and graceful, particularly those of women and children, with the limbs true to nature, as in the case of men, but veiled with a plumpness and fleshiness that should not be awkward, as they are in nature, but refined by draughtsmanship and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render flesh with refined softness—figures should be true to nature yet subtly idealized (veiled plumpness), especially for women and children, to produce grace rather than awkward realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance of costume, variety, colouring, and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: They also lacked our abundance of beautiful costumes, our great number and variety of bizarre fancies, loveliness of colouring, wide knowledge of buildings, and distance and variety in landscapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enrich compositions with varied and beautiful costume design, inventive ornament, rich colouring, architectural knowledge, and diverse landscape backgrounds to increase pictorial interest and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolute boldness / spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: If they had had that minuteness of finish which is the perfection and bloom of art, they would also have had a resolute boldness in their works; and from this there would have followed delicacy, refinement, and supreme grace...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courageous, decisive handling (boldness) in composition and technique is a mark of mastery and leads to refined grace; lack of boldness produces weakness in manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety in counterfeiting the minutiesses of nature (Leonardo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo... giving a beginning to that third manner which we propose to call the modern--besides the force and boldness of his drawing, and the extreme subtlety wherewith he counterfeited all the minutiesses of nature exactly as they are...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue extreme subtlety and micro-observation—capture the small, exact details of nature (textures, small forms) to achieve a modern realism and expressive power, as exemplified by Leonardo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion and breath in figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo... may be truly said to have endowed his figures with motion and breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose figures to convey life, movement, and animation—pose, gesture, and subtle modelling should give the appearance of living, breathing presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chiaroscuro and use of deep shadow to increase relief
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an extraordinary thing how that genius, in his desire to give the highest relief to the works that he made, went so far with dark shadows, in order to find the darkest possible grounds, that he sought for blacks which might make deeper shadows and be darker than other blacks, that by their means he might make his lights the brighter; and in the end this method turned out so dark...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong contrasts and deep shadows (chiaroscuro) to enhance modelling and relief—seek dark grounds and deep blacks to make lights read brighter, but be aware of the danger of over-darkening that can obscure daylight qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradation of colour, force, relief, and softness of hair (colour handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Giorgione... obtained a beautiful gradation of colour in his pictures, and gave a sublime movement to his works by means of a certain darkness of shadow... Antonio da Correggio... painted hair in detail... soft and feathery, with each single hair visible... giving force, relief, sweetness, and grace to his pictures, with his colouring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ subtle colour gradation, soft modelling, and detailed handling (even of hair) to produce relief, sweetness, and movement; colouring is central to conveying form and emotional tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative vividness and natural truth in painted stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Raffaello... his painted stories, which are as vivid as writings, for in them he showed us places and buildings true to reality, and the features and costumes both of our own people and of strangers... his invention was facile and peculiar to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose narrative scenes with clarity and lived realism—accurate depiction of settings, costumes, and expressive gestures makes painted stories 'vivid as writings'; imagination should be facile but grounded in observed truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshortening and handling difficult poses
rubrics_metrics.description: They sought with great efforts to do the impossible in art by means of labour, particularly in foreshortenings and in things unpleasant to the eye, which were as painful to see as they were difficult for them to execute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master challenging pictorial problems (foreshortening, extreme poses) through diligent study and technique; successful handling of such difficulties is a mark of skill, though over-laboured attempts can produce strain or unpleasantness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological expression and depiction of inner states
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Last Supper... he succeeded in expressing that anxiety which had seized the Apostles in wishing to know who should betray their Master. For which reason in all their faces are seen love, fear, and wrath, or rather, sorrow... in contrast... obstinacy, hatred, and treachery in Judas...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict subtle and varied psychological states across figures to communicate the narrative tension and inner life of subjects; facial expression and grouping should convey distinct emotions appropriate to each character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish versus productivity (execution and polish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherefore those early masters took six years to paint one panel, our modern masters can paint six in one year... our pictures are clearly much more highly finished and perfect than those executed in former times by masters of account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for an efficient practice that does not sacrifice finish and perfection; modern methods and skill can increase productivity while achieving high finish, but finish remains a central measure of quality.
